items.q: What is the difference between a trace and an eval?
items.a: A trace is a **detailed log of every agent step**; an eval is **a test run on those traces** for outputs that are never the same twice.

items.q: Why isn't trying your agent a few times enough?
items.a: **Looks good to me is not a test suite**: three tries miss regressions, and every prompt change can break **inputs you never tested**.

items.q: What are the three kinds of evals?
items.a: **Code evals** for deterministic checks, **LLM judges** for meaning, and **human review** for new failures and judge calibration.

items.q: What should you do before writing any eval?
items.a: **Read a dozen traces end to end** and note what went wrong, so you measure **what matters, not what's easy**.

items.q: What are open and axial coding?
items.a: **Open coding** is writing free notes on each trace; **axial coding** groups those notes into **failure categories** afterwards.

items.q: How do you prioritise which failure to fix first?
items.a: Multiply **frequency × severity**: a rare but dangerous output beats a common minor one.

items.q: Why diagnose the cause and not just the wrong answer?
items.a: A wrong answer is a symptom; **retrieval, reasoning, hallucination and scope** failures each need **a different fix**.

items.q: What goes into a good LLM judge prompt?
items.a: **Role and context**, explicit criteria from your error analysis, **XML-wrapped data**, labelled examples, and a **constrained answer**.

items.q: What biases do LLM judges have?
items.a: **Position, length, confidence and self-preference** bias; judge with a **stronger, different-provider model**.

items.q: Should a judge favour precision or recall?
items.a: Usually **recall**: a false alarm costs a minute, but **a missed failure reaches the customer**.

items.q: What is a god evaluator and why avoid it?
items.a: One prompt checking everything; when it fails **you can't tell what failed**, so use **one evaluator per dimension**.

items.q: What makes an eval most useful?
items.a: An **even pass/fail split** gives a **hill to climb**; all-pass or all-fail teaches nothing.

items.q: What happens to an eval once it passes reliably?
items.a: It becomes a **regression eval** in CI: guardrails must pass, north stars gate on an **average like 0.8**.

items.q: What did upgrading Haiku 4.5 to 5.5 reveal?
items.a: Faithfulness **tripled** but cost **4×**, and it got consistent by **answering hold almost every time**.
